The reviews and discussions on the manuscript highlighted both strengths and weaknesses.

On the one hand, the manuscript contributes to the literature studying quantization and pruning in randomly initialized neural networks, particularly how much overparametrization is needed such that the resulting subnetwork exactly reproduces a finite-precision target network. While earlier SLTH works handled continuous weights or required binary targets, the paper proves that pruning alone can yield subnetworks that exactly realize arbitrary finite-precision targets across a wide range of quantisation levels.

On the other hand, the submitted manuscript has significant drawbacks requiring a rather substantial revision. There is a need to improve the manuscript, addressing questions like why the considered problem is interesting (this is relative to target audience), why and how are the assumptions justified, giving illustrating examples so on. There is a need also to clarify the contributions of the work, interpretation of results, and scope of the considered setting and assumptions. Other concerns have pointed out the need to improve with empirical validations or simulation-based experiments, discussion on the practical achievability of the assumed quantization precision, connection to existing quantization frameworks, implications for practical situations, among other.

Upon balancing strengths and weaknesses, my conclusion is that the submitted manuscript didn't fully meet the high-quality standards of NeurIPS, as another round of reviewing would be required before confidently accepting the paper. The authors are strongly encouraged to resubmit an improved version to a forthcoming venue.

First, we would like to remark that we have fully addressed the **theoretical** concerns raised by reviewer U5bx, who didn't ask for any additional questions after our clarifications. We are more than eager to clarify any additional doubts. 

Regarding the **practicality** of the assumptions, we acknowledge the importance of further clarifying them in the introduction of our paper, which we commit to do. The lack of detailed discussion on the fact that **our assumptions are considered realistic with respect to practical scenarios** (specifically regarding the broad class of weight distributions for which our results hold), is due to the fact that such assumptions are essentially the same as those made in the existing literature on SLTH (we refer to our paper for a quick review of the many papers that have been published on the subject at NeurIPS and related conferences over several years). The main difference in our case is that we consider the quantized (discretized) setting; however, our results still encompass any weight distribution considered in practice (be it Glorot Uniform, Kaiming Uniform, Glorot Normal, He Normal, LeCun Normal, and so on). It is important to remark that changing the initial distribution from uniform (which we assume for simplicity's sake) to other distributions, **only requires a small constant factor in the final result** (as shown in the original paper by [Lueker 1998], and subsequently in [Pensia et al. 2020] and subsequent SLTH works. Finally, we emphasize that our results (and previous ones), only assume that the support of the initial  distribution **contains** a connected interval around its center. This is specifically discussed in [Lueker 1998], where it was shown for the first time that the standard rejection-sampling argument still allow to handle distributions such as, for example, a truncated normal distribution (which could additionally have holes outside a standard deviation from the origin); again, this would only incur a relatively small constant factor on the overall number of weights (whereas general lower bounds show that the necessary overparameterization is of logarithmic order).  

More broadly, we would like to emphasize that the central aim of our paper is to explore the following question: Given the standard assumptions used in prior work, what are the implications of quantizing network weights and activations? Specifically, how do the results depend on the level of precision? We have successfully answered this question by deriving the explicit dependence on precision. This is a practically very relevant issue that has been left open in the SLTH literature so far, since in the real world, computers cannot represent numbers with infinite precision—real numbers do not exist in actual computation. In this sense, our work addresses an important practical limitation in the application of previous SLTH results, and does so **without introducing any new assumption** regarding the weight distribution or other aspects mentioned so far in the reviews.
Certainly, there are issues that remain open in the SLTH literature, and that we aim to discuss in our conclusion section (which will include some additional content, as discussed in our rebuttals). However, we firmly believe that the whole theoretical community working on SLTH would agree that each of those remaining issues is worth a full paper in itself.

I would like to thank the authors for their responses. After reviewing their answers to my and other reviewers’ questions, as well as the discussion with reviewer U5bx, I have become increasingly convinced that the practical applicability of the findings may be significantly limited. The assumption of a uniform weight distribution, even when extended via rejection sampling, appears too strong for real, trained networks, which typically exhibit highly structured, sparse, and non-uniform weight distributions. In this regard, I find myself in agreement with reviewer U5bx, and I reiterate that the paper would benefit greatly from empirical validation to demonstrate the practical relevance of the theoretical bounds.

To make a final decision, I would appreciate clarification on the following point:

Your proof relies on rejection sampling to extend the result from uniform to non-uniform weight distributions. However, this technique requires the target distribution to have full support over the entire quantized set $𝑆_{\delta}$, and it can drastically increase the required size of the initial network due to rejected samples. Given that real, trained networks typically exhibit highly structured, sparse, and peaked weight distributions that often lack full support, how do you reconcile the practical feasibility of your optimal bounds with these deviations from your theoretical assumptions?

We thank the reviewer for articulating their remaining concerns regarding our assumptions.

(i) As pointed out in our response to Reviewer JJR5, our results hold for essentially any weight distribution of practical interest. Different distributions for the larger network can be addressed using rejection sampling, as shown in our current proof of Lemma 5. The uniform distribution was chosen solely for illustrative purposes. We will add a corresponding remark in the paper.

(ii) We know that for a given set, an RSSP can be solved if $\kappa < 1$, 
or equivalently if $n > \log\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$, with probability at least $1 - \mathcal{O}\left(n^{-\frac{1}{7}}\right)$. 
The reviewer's concern is whether this $n$ is too large and whether the probability is sufficiently high in practical settings. However, the condition $n > \log\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$ is not demanding: it essentially states that $n$ must exceed the number of bits required to represent the target (up to a constant factor), which is largely satisfied in practice: real networks commonly uses 32 bits per weight and, in the context of quantization, typically less than 16, while they contain a number of weigths per layer that ranges from 100k to more than 10 millions, which easily meet the $n \gg \log(1/\delta)$ condition.

We hope these clarifications address the reviewer’s concern about the applicability of our result. Should further detail be required, we would be glad to provide it.

We thank the reviewer for their precious feedback. 

## Response to the questions

**Question 1**

The SLTH has already been theoretically established and/or empirically validated for CNNs, Graph Transformers, and several other architectures, [Cunha and Natale, 2022], [Ito et al. 2025]. Using our methods, one could aim to extend these results to a quantized setting for various architectures. This is a promising direction for future work. As discussed in the response to Reviewer JJR5, we also acknowledge that we have not included an experimental validation of our results, since our work is itself motivated by the empirical results of [Diffenderfer et al. 2021]. We kindly defer the reviewer to that discussion for more details. 

**Question 2**

There is no issue in having different $\gamma$ values for different layers, as long as they satisfy the required assumptions. In our work, we chose the largest possible $\gamma$ to allow for maximum quantization, but using smaller values is perfectly acceptable. We agree that for the first result (Theorem 1), we require layers that do not reset the precision—this assumption was made for theoretical simplicity. In Theorem 2, only one such layer is needed, and the remaining layers are unrestricted. Removing such assumptions and generalizing the results further is an important direction for future work.

**Question 3**

In this work, we represent a given target network by pruning and quantizing a larger network, without involving any training. Moreover, we obtain an exact representation of the smaller network. These facts implies that, in our case, there is no issue of quantization variance reduction. We remark that our setup is standard in the SLTH line of theoretical research. While we acknowledge that the setting is somewhat idealized, it is the first work to establish a formal relationship between quantization and pruning. We hope that our theoretical progress will pave the way to advancements that weakens the aforementioned assumptions. 

## **References**
Arthur Cunha and Emanuele Natale. Proving the lottery ticket hypothesis for convolutional neural networks. In ICLR, 2022.

Hiroaki Ito, Jiale Yan, Hikari Otsuka, Kazushi Kawamura, Masato Motomura, Thiem Van Chu, and Daichi Fujiki. Uncovering strong lottery tickets in graph transformers: A path to memory efficient and robust graph learning, In TMLR, 2025.

James Diffenderfer and Bhavya Kailkhura. Multi-prize lottery ticket hypothesis: Finding accurate binary neural networks by pruning a randomly weighted network. In ICLR, 2021.

## Response to the questions

**Question 1**

We acknowledge that, similarly to other theoretical works on the SLTH, we have not provided an experimental validation of our results, the reason being that such theoretical research direction has been motivated by previous experimental work as seen in [Ramanujan et al. 2020] and [Diffenderfer et al. 2021] (we refer to the references in our paper). 
[Diffenderfer et al. 2021] in particular, provide empirical validation for our findings through their pruning method, whereas the primary goal of our work is to prove the mathematical limits and possibility of such approaches. On the other hand, we emphasize that our results are general and are not limited to the method by Diffenderfer et al. The most interesting future direction, in this respect, would be to test different methods, including computationally-intensive approaches for small networks, in order to compare the various approaches against the theoretical limits provided by our results; such extensive experiments are, however, beyond the scope of the present paper. We will add more details regarding the interest of such investigations in our conclusion section.

**Question 2**

We thank the reviewer for making us realize that we did not discuss, in our introduction, such important aspect of our work: in fact, our results hold for essentially any weight distribution of practical interest. Although, for simplicity's sake, we initially assume a uniform weight distribution, we later employ a standard rejection-sampling argument  for taking care of the non-uniform distributions that arise later in our technical proofs. Such argument can, in fact, be employed from the very beginning, to make the proof holds for any distribution that "contains" a uniform one. This technique has already be used in [Lueker 1998] and [Pensia et al. 2020], among others, and holds in our case as well. 

**Question 3**

Establishing clear connections with real-world pruning heuristics remains an open and important question for future work. On the one hand, our theoretical bounds hold for any pruning method, including brute-force approaches. On the other hand, while a brute-force approaches would be infeasible, our results indicate the existence of a phase transition, suggesting that some heuristics could approach the optimal solution. Providing a clear connection in this sense, however, entails making progress on the theoretical understanding of magnitude pruning methods and alike, which is beyond the scope of our current contributions.

We thank the reviewer for their precious feedback. The points identified as mistakes are due to some confusion in the statement of lemma 5 and some other imprecisions. Below are our clarifications regarding the concerns raised.  We are grateful to the reviewer for highlighting these issues and we will address them as explained below. 

In light of such clarifications, please let us know their revised evaluation of our work. We are obviously eager to provide any additional explanation, should they require it.  

## 1. On the apparently missing union-bound over all target weights in Lemma 5.
Indeed, we are not proving that the statement holds for all weights in $S_{\delta}$, but rather for any single weight sampled from $S_{\delta}$ (i.e., exactly what we currently prove). We are thankful to the reviewer for pointing this out and will revise the statement accordingly: rather than saying "[...] with high probability, for all weights we have [...]", the correct form is "[...] for any weight, with high probability we have [...]". 

Specifically, Lemma 5 establishes that, under certain conditions, a neural network with only a single weight—i.e., a linear function mapping input $x$ to output $wx$ (ignoring precision resets) — can be represented by pruning a large network. 
The value of this target weight is uniformly sampled from $w$ from the discrete set $S_{\delta}$. This construction reduces the problem to that of solving a Random Subset Sum Problem (RSSP) with a *single* target value $w$.
We remark that this is a weaker requirement than what is often proven in the RSSP literature (e.g. in the seminal result [Lueker, 1998], in the references of our paper), where the existence of a subset is guaranteed for all targets simultaneously. Similarly to previous SLTH results (e.g. [Natale et al., 2024]), such  stronger version is not necessary in our case. Our Lemma 4 provides the probability of solving an RSSP for *any single* target sampled from $S_{\delta}$ (without requiring a solution for all possible targets simultaneously), which is sufficient to prove our results.


## 2. On the validity of Lemma 4 outside the given asymptotic regime.
The reviewer points out that we assume the condition $\kappa < 1$ for a high-probability guarantee. Such assumption is in fact necessary, as a corollary of previous results by [Borgs et al, 2001].
We will either revise the statement of Lemma 4, or add a remark afterwards, noting that the condition is not only sufficient but necessary. 

As for the constant $C$, let us recall where it comes from. It is known that RSSP can be solved with high probability if $\kappa < 1$, or equivalently, $n > \log\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$. However, in the typical scenarios of interest in our case, the samples encountered are not uniformly distributed. To address this, we take a larger number of samples—specifically, $n > C \log\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$—and then apply a rejection sampling argument to recover uniformly distributed samples. We thus assume $C > 1$, and we will make such assumption explicit in the paper.

Regarding the asymptotic nature of the results: if $n$ grows faster than $C \log\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$, the probability of solving the problem converges to 1, and we also characterize the *rate* at which this convergence occurs. For any finite $n$, we can thus quantify the probability of success. 
We do believe that the true convergence rate should be exponential rather than polynomial in $n$. Such rate cannot however be achieved with our current approach. We will add this open problem as an important challenge in our conclusion section. 

Regarding the limitations section, they are currently mentioned in the conclusion of the paper. We acknowledge that our results are proved under certain assumptions, but we believe these assumptions are not fundamental obstacles and can likely be relaxed or generalized in future work. We are considering the possibility to move them to a standalone section (at the price of some other sections, because of paper length constraints), for better clarity.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for their precious feedback. 
We acknowledge that, like most results in this area, our contributions are existential in nature and primarily offer theoretical guarantees, without directly providing practical guidance for pruning and quantizing neural networks. However, we believe that such theoretical insights represent meaningful progress and are valuable for advancing the foundational understanding in this field. For our perspective on the connection to experiments, please refer to our response to Reviewer JJR5, who shared a similar point. 

## Response to the question
This appears to be a misunderstanding—there is no layer collapse involved. In fact, we consider two distinct neural networks: one with $\ell$ layers and another with $2\ell$ layers. We allow pruning of the larger network, and the central question is whether this can be done such that the pruned $2\ell$-layer network produces the same output as the $\ell$-layer network for any input. Both networks are given at the outset. We prune some weights from the larger network (but never entire layers). As a result, the $\ell$-layer network remains $\ell$-layered, and the $2\ell$-layer network remains $2\ell$-layer. The pruning is performed in such a way that, for every input, both networks produce the same output—thereby representing the same function.
Please let us know if they would like any further clarification; we are eager to provide them.

summary.value: This paper extends the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (SLTH) to the setting of quantized neural networks, showing theoretically that large, randomly initialized finite-precision networks contain sparse subnetworks that can exactly match any target quantized network. By bridging ideas from SSP and NNP, this paper proves very tight optimal bounds on the required overparameterization. For the first time, this paper has shown that pruning alone can yield exact finite-precision subnetworks rather than merely approximate ones, closing a key theoretical gap in neural network compression.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

Based on the literature reviewed here, this work is the first one that provides a new, sharp bounds for the discret RSSP and proves that pruning can yield exact, not just approximate, quantized subnetworks.

The writing is in general very clean, especially the introduction and the related work.

Weaknesses:
The proof of the bounds appears quite reasonable and well-motivated. I wonder if it would be possible to use these theoretical bounds more directly to guide practical quantization and pruning methods in real networks?

questions.value:
In Theorem 1, the paper claims that with high probability, a depth-$2ℓ$ network can be quantized to precision $\delta$ and then pruned to yield a functionally equivalent precision-$\delta_t$ depth-ℓ network. However, this implies that pruning discards entire layers to reduce the depth. In practice, for a standard MLP as assumed in the proof, removing whole layers would collapse the structure of the network and break the feedforward flow. Could the authors clarify how this depth reduction should be interpreted for practical architectures?

summary.value: The paper develops tight theory showing how much over-parameterization a randomly initialized network needs to be so that, after quantizing its weights and then pruning them, the resulting subnetwork can exactly reproduce any finite-precision target network. By leveraging phase-transition results for the discrete Number Partitioning Problem, the authors prove that a depth-2ℓ network of width $O\bigl(d\log(1/\delta)\bigr)$ can, with high probability, be reduced to precision δ and pruned to implement any δ\_t-quantized network of width ≤ d; a matching parameter-counting lower bound shows the logarithmic factor is optimal. This extends the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis from continuous weights to the fully discrete setting by recasting pruning as a quantized Random Subset Sum problem and deriving new bounds that survive outside the asymptotic regime assumed in earlier work. Consequently, pruning alone—without any weight training—can yield subnetworks that exactly match the desired finite-precision function, closing the gap between achievable and information-theoretic limits for quantized SLTH.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
## Strength:

1. Unlike earlier SLTH work that handled continuous weights or required binary targets, the paper proves that pruning alone can yield subnetworks that exactly realise arbitrary finite-precision targets across a wide range of quantisation levels, closing the gap left by prior cubic-over-parameterisation results.

2. By importing phase-transition results from the classical Number Partitioning Problem to sharpen bounds for the discrete Random Subset-Sum Problem, the study introduces a fresh combinatorial toolkit to network compression theory, demonstrating how ideas from statistical physics and combinatorics can unlock new deep-learning results.

## Weakness:




1. Missing union-bound over all target weights in Lemma 5: 


Lemma 5 first shows that for one fixed target weight w a Subset-Sum instance is solvable with probability
$p = 1-\varepsilon = 1-O((\log_2 1/\delta)^{-1/7})$.
But the statement of the lemma requires the property to hold simultaneously for every weight
$w\in S_{\delta_t}$, where
$|S_{\delta_t}| = 2/\delta_t+1 = \Theta(2^{k_t})$ can be exponentially large.
A union bound over all those targets is therefore mandatory:

$$
\Pr\bigl(\exists w\ \text{that fails}\bigr)\;\le\;|S_{\delta_t}|\,(1-p)
      =\Theta(2^{k_t})\,O\!\bigl((\log_2 1/\delta)^{-1/7}\bigr),
$$

which is **not** $O((\log_2 1/\delta)^{-1/7})$ unless $\delta_t$ itself is exponentially small.
Without this extra factor the claimed “high-probability” guarantee is vacuous.



2. Applying Lemma 4 outside its asymptotic regime

Inside Lemma 5 the authors invoke Lemma 4 to say that a Random Subset-Sum with
$n\ge 2\log_2(1/\delta)$ items succeeds with probability
$1-O\!\bigl((\log_2 1/\delta)^{-1/7}\bigr)$ .

Lemma 4 itself, however, is proved only for the thermodynamic regime
$n\to\infty$ with

$$
\kappa_n=\frac{\log_2 M}{n}<1
$$

In the instantiation used in Lemma 5 we have
$M=1/\delta$ and $n=C\log_2(1/\delta)$, so

$$
\kappa_n=\frac{\log_2(1/\delta)}{C\log_2(1/\delta)}=\frac1C,
$$

which indeed is $<1$ only if $C>1$.
Yet the proof never chooses a numerical $C$; more importantly,
Lemma 4’s bound becomes meaningful only for *large* n (needed for the Hoeffding tail and the moment estimates).
With $n$ merely logarithmic in $1/\delta$ that asymptotic argument does **not** yield the stated polynomial-in-log failure probability, so the central success probability $p$ is unsupported.



Both the depth-2 and the $(\ell\!+\!1)$-layer constructions simply stack Lemma 5 (via Lemma 6 & 7) and then union-bound over every neuron and layer.
Because Lemma 5’s probability bound is already overstated, multiplying it by the number of neurons makes the final “with high probability” claim untenable; in realistic parameter ranges the resulting lower bound on success probability can even become negative, so Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are not proved.

questions.value:
1. In Lemma 5 the success probability is stated for every target weight $w\in S_{\delta_t}$, yet the proof only analyses one fixed $w$. How would you tighten the argument (e.g., via an explicit union bound or a refined concentration inequality) so that the bound still holds when $|S_{\delta_t}|$ is exponential in $1/\delta_t$?

2. Lemma 4 is invoked with $n = C\log_2(1/\delta)$ items, which is far from the large-$n$ limit in which the phase-transition estimates were derived. Could you provide a non-asymptotic analysis—or empirical evidence—that the claimed $O((\log 1/\delta)^{-1/7})$ failure probability remains valid for these logarithmic widths?

summary.value: The paper explores the relationship between quantization and pruning within the framework of the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (SLTH). The authors establish theoretical bounds on the degree of overparameterization required for a randomly initialized, finite-precision neural network to contain subnetworks that can exactly replicate the functionality of a target quantized model. By extending prior results from continuous to discrete settings, the work leverages insights from the Number Partitioning Problem (NPP) and the Random Subset Sum Problem (RSSP). The central contribution is a formal proof that, under suitable quantization constraints, pruning alone is sufficient to recover exact representations of quantized networks, along with tight bounds on the size of the overparameterized network required for this recovery.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### **Strengths And Weaknesses**

**Strengths**
The paper makes a strong theoretical contribution by rigorously analyzing the quantized RSSP and linking it to the SLTH framework. The presentation is coherent, and the results are derived from classical yet well-established combinatorial problems. The work is self-contained and addresses the theoretical problem comprehensively, without deferring essential details to future work. This provides a clear conceptual basis for future algorithmic development in the area of neural network quantization and pruning.

**Weaknesses**
However, the paper does not include any empirical validation or simulation-based experiments. This absence may reduce the paper’s accessibility and practical impact, particularly for readers more interested in applied aspects. The connection between theory and practice, while suggestive, remains abstract. Even minimal experiments (e.g., on small-scale networks, in the spirit of the original Lottery Ticket Hypothesis) would significantly increase the paper's relevance and demonstrate the utility of the theoretical findings. While the core analytical tools are classical, their application in this context is original.


### **Comments on quality, clarity, significance and originality**

**Quality**
The paper is technically sound and provides a solid theoretical contribution to the study of neural network compression. The mathematical derivations are rigorous and complete. However, the lack of empirical or simulation-based validation is a notable shortcoming. Given that the theoretical framework could likely be applied in simplified setups, such an omission feels like a missed opportunity to increase the paper’s practical credibility.

**Clarity**
The manuscript is clearly written and well-organized. The theoretical background, problem formulation, and derivations are presented in a logical order. Mathematical notation is precise, and the arguments are easy to follow for readers with a background in theoretical machine learning or combinatorics.

**Significance**
The theoretical insights presented have the potential to influence future work on training-free network compression strategies. However, the practical significance remains speculative, as no empirical evidence is provided to support the theoretical claims. A broader audience might find it difficult to assess the real-world relevance of the results without some form of validation.

**Originality**
The synthesis of classical combinatorial results with modern deep learning theory is original and intellectually valuable. While the foundational components (NPP, RSSP) are not new, their integration into the SLTH framework and the exploration of quantization’s role represents a novel and worthwhile contribution. The derivation of tight bounds for finite-precision networks represents a meaningful departure from earlier continuous approximations.

questions.value:
1. While the focus of the paper is theoretical, have the authors considered performing any small-scale empirical validation? Such experiments could help demonstrate the practical relevance of the derived bounds.

2. The theoretical analysis relies on the assumption of uniform sampling from the quantized weight set. How well does this assumption reflect typical weight distributions observed in trained neural networks? Could deviations from uniformity affect the applicability of the results?

3. The combinatorial formulation used in the theoretical construction differs from practical pruning strategies. How do the authors envision their results relating to common pruning methods such as magnitude pruning or iterative pruning? Are there potential pathways to bridge these theoretical insights with real-world pruning heuristics?

summary.value:
This theoretical work extends the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis to the quantized domain. It demonstrates that an analogous class of target discrete neural networks can be exactly represented within this setting. The study also establishes optimal bounds for the necessary over-parameterization of the initial network, which are dependent on the precision of the target network.

The research focuses on the theoretical over-parameterization required to achieve quantized strong lottery tickets. This foundational theory is crucial for guiding future model compression efforts. The concluding theorem indicates that the optimal solution for model compression is bounded by \\Omega(dlog(1/\\delta)) parameters. Furthermore, network depth can be reduced to l+1, at the cost of an additional log(1/\\delta) factor in network width.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
* This paper offers a theoretical discussion on the extent to which large neural networks can compress a target neural network under quantization, serving as an effective extension of the existing SLTH framework to cover more general cases. This fundamental technical discussion promises long-term benefits for the community.
* The work provides concrete theoretical proof for quantized RSSP and revisits classical results on RNPP. New theorems on quantized SLTH are also presented, building upon the established theorems. The overall structure of the statements is clear and detailed.

title.value: Quantization vs Pruning: Insights from the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis

abstract.value:
Quantization is an essential technique for making neural networks more efficient, yet our theoretical understanding of it remains limited. Previous works demonstrated that extremely low-precision networks, such as binary networks, can be constructed by pruning large, randomly-initialized networks, and showed that the ratio between the size of the original and the pruned networks is at most polylogarithmic.  
The specific pruning method they employed inspired a line of theoretical work known as the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (SLTH), which leverages insights from the Random Subset Sum Problem. However, these results primarily address the continuous setting and cannot be applied to extend SLTH results to the quantized setting. 
In this work, we build on foundational results by Borgs et al. on the Number Partitioning Problem to derive new theoretical results for the Random Subset Sum Problem in a quantized setting.  
Using these results, we then extend the SLTH framework to finite-precision networks. While prior work on SLTH showed that pruning allows approximation of a certain class of neural networks, we demonstrate that, in the quantized setting, the analogous class of target discrete neural networks can be represented exactly, and we prove optimal bounds on the necessary overparameterization of the initial network as a function of the precision of the target network.

TLDR.value: We provide optimal relationships between the network size and weight precision of a large network such that it can be pruned to a given target network.
